title: How to Build a Healthy Church Staff Culture
excerpt: The staff culture you actually have is the one you tolerate on a Tuesday, not the one you describe in the elder retreat.
body:
A staff meeting opens with prayer, and three of the five people praying are afraid of the person leading it. They are not afraid he will yell. They are afraid of something quieter than that. They are afraid of the look that crosses his face when someone disagrees, the way the temperature in the room drops two degrees, the email that comes at nine that night with the subject line that just says 'Quick thought.' So they pray, and they smile, and they keep the real conversation for the parking lot. The culture of that staff is not the printed values on the breakroom wall. The culture is what happens in the parking lot.

Most pastors think they are building a healthy staff culture when what they are building is a comfortable one. The two are not the same. A comfortable culture is a place where nobody contradicts the leader and everyone leaves on time and the conflict goes underground where it ferments. A healthy culture is a place where the hardest thing on the table gets said by the person least afraid to say it, and nobody loses standing for saying it. I have run both kinds. I know the difference from the inside, because for years I mistook the silence in my own staff meetings for peace, and it was not peace. It was the absence of trust dressed up as agreement.

Let me steel-man the comfortable manager, because he is not a villain and he is often me. He has read the studies. He knows that turnover in ministry is brutal, that pastors burn out, that a church split can take a decade to heal. So he protects the calm. He smooths the friction. He tells himself that a peaceful staff is a faithful staff, that unity is a fruit of the Spirit, that he is shepherding tender people through a hard calling. And he is right about the tenderness. He is right that people in ministry carry wounds that the corporate world does not see. The instinct to protect them is a good instinct that has been pointed in the wrong direction.

Here is what he gets wrong. He has confused the absence of conflict with the presence of trust, and Patrick Lencioni spent a career showing that these are nearly opposites (Lencioni 2002). Trust is what makes conflict survivable. Where trust is high, people fight about ideas in the open and walk out of the room intact. Where trust is low, people agree in the room and undermine in the hallway. The peaceful staff the comfortable manager is so proud of is not a sign of trust. It is a sign that trust is so thin nobody dares to test it. He is not protecting his people. He is starving them of the one thing that would let them tell him the truth.

The spine text here is the night before the cross, and it is stranger than we let it be. 'Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist' (John 13:3-4 ESV). Read the logic of that sentence. John tells us first that Jesus knew the full extent of his authority, that everything had been placed in his hands, and then, because of that knowledge and not in spite of it, he got on the floor and washed twelve sets of dirty feet. The security came first. The service came out of the security. He could kneel because there was nothing left to prove.

That is the engine of a healthy staff culture, and almost nobody runs on it. The leader who knows where his standing comes from can take the lowest seat in the room without losing himself. The leader who does not know is the one who needs the meeting to affirm him, who cannot let a critique pass without correcting the record, who washes nobody's feet because he is still waiting for someone to wash his. A church staff inherits the anxiety of the person at the top. If the senior leader is grasping, the whole staff grasps. If he can kneel, he gives them permission to stop performing.

We did not get here by accident, and the history matters. The modern church staff is a young invention. For most of Christian history the local congregation had a pastor and perhaps a sexton, and the idea of an executive pastor, a creative director, a connections coordinator, and a discipleship pastor reporting through an org chart would have been unintelligible. The multi-staff church as we know it is largely a product of the church growth movement that took shape in the nineteen seventies and eighties, when Donald McGavran's work at Fuller and the rise of the seeker-sensitive megachurch taught a generation to think of the congregation as an organization to be scaled. We imported the org chart from the corporation, and with it we imported the corporation's diseases, the politics, the performance reviews, the quiet anxiety of people whose livelihood depends on a manager's mood.

None of that is wrong in itself. Structure is a gift. But we adopted the structure without adopting the safeguard, and the safeguard is theological, not managerial. Edwin Friedman, a rabbi who spent his life studying leadership in congregations and families, named the missing piece. He called it self-differentiation, the capacity of a leader to stay connected to people while staying clear about his own convictions, to hold steady in the presence of someone else's anxiety without absorbing it or reacting to it (Friedman 2007). The differentiated leader does not need the staff to be calm in order to be calm himself. That is what lets him invite the hard conversation. He can hear it without coming apart.

So what do you actually do. Begin with the thing you can control, which is your own face in the room. Watch what happens to the temperature when someone disagrees with you, and learn to keep it level on purpose, because the staff is reading you for permission and you are giving it whether you mean to or not. Then make the disagreement count for something. When a junior staff member tells you a plan will not work and she is right, change the plan in front of everyone and say out loud who changed your mind. Nothing teaches a staff that candor is safe faster than watching candor win once. Bonhoeffer warned that the leader who arrives with a vision of the perfect community and demands that the real people conform to it will end up destroying both the vision and the people (Bonhoeffer 1954). Lead the staff you have, not the one in your head.

And ration your reactions. Henri Nouwen wrote that the great temptation of Christian leadership is the temptation to be relevant, to be spectacular, to be powerful, and that the antidote is a leadership that descends rather than climbs, that is willing to be led where it would rather not go (Nouwen 1989). A healthy staff culture is built by a leader who has made peace with not being the most impressive person in the room. He does not need the win in every exchange. He has already washed feet. He has nothing to prove and therefore everything to give.

There is a test for whether the culture is actually changing, and it is a quiet one. Listen for what your newest and least powerful staff member is willing to say in front of the room. The intern, the part-time administrator, the young hire who joined six months ago and has the most to lose by speaking. When that person disagrees with you out loud, without lowering her voice and without checking the faces of the older staff first, you have built something real. Until that day, every assurance that your people feel free to speak is a thing you are telling yourself, not a thing they have shown you. The health of a staff is measured at its bottom, not its top, the same way Jesus measured greatness on the night he reached for the towel.

The culture you have is the one your people describe in the parking lot. You will not change it with a values document or a ropes course or a verse on the wall. You will change it the first time someone says the dangerous true thing in the meeting and watches you receive it without flinching. That is the whole work, and it never ends. The towel does not stay tied. You pick it up again every Tuesday.

A healthy staff is not a quiet one. It is a brave one.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Lencioni, Patrick. 2002. The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

title: When to Fire Someone in Ministry
excerpt: The cruelest thing a pastor can do to a staff member is keep him on a year past the point where everyone but him already knows.
body:
The conversation everyone is dreading has already happened a hundred times. It has happened in the car on the way home, when the executive pastor's wife asked how it went and he said nothing and stared at the road. It has happened in the elder meeting, in the long pause after someone says his name. It has happened in the worship leader's own gut at two in the morning. The only place it has not happened is the one place it needs to happen, which is across a desk, in daylight, with the words said plainly. We will keep almost anyone for almost any length of time to avoid that one room.

Firing someone in ministry is harder than firing someone anywhere else, and we should say why instead of pretending otherwise. In a normal job, the relationship is contractual. In a church, the relationship is covenantal, or it feels that way. You prayed together. You buried his father. His kids call you by a nickname. You stood in front of the congregation and said God had called this person to this work, and now you are sitting across from him preparing to say it is over. The language of calling and the language of employment are tangled together, and we use the tangle as an excuse to do nothing.

Let me give the case for patience its full strength, because it is a strong case and I have hidden behind it. Grace is the center of what we preach. We believe people can change. We believe the Spirit is not finished with anyone. We have all known a leader who was struggling in month eight and thriving in month twenty, and we are right to fear the kind of pastor who fires fast and prays slow. Scripture is full of restoration, of Peter rebuilt on a beach after he had failed at the worst possible moment. A church that cuts its people loose at the first sign of weakness is not a church, it is a firm with a steeple. The patient pastor is protecting something real.

But grace and clarity are not enemies, and we treat them as if they were. The patient pastor has performed a sleight of hand on himself. He has decided that keeping the failing staff member is the gracious choice, when in fact it is often the cowardly one wearing grace as a costume. Grace toward the underperforming worship leader is not the only grace in the room. There is also the grace owed to the volunteers he is exhausting, the grace owed to the congregation he is no longer serving, the grace owed to the man himself, who deserves to know the truth while he is still young enough to find the thing he is actually built for. By calling my avoidance grace, I was spending other people's grace to protect my own comfort.

The text I want to carry is the appointing of the seven in Acts, because it shows that ministry roles exist for a function and not as a reward. The widows were being neglected in the daily distribution, and the apostles did not say the men currently failing at the task deserved patience. They said the work had to be done, and they sought out men full of the Spirit and of wisdom to do it (Acts 6:3 ESV). The role served the people. When the role stops serving the people, the role has to change hands, and the kindness is owed first to the people the role exists for. We have inverted this. We treat the staff position as belonging to the staff member, a possession we would be cruel to take away, when it was never his. It was the congregation's, on loan.

So when. Not for one bad season, and not for a personality you find tiring, and never for telling you the truth you did not want to hear. Fire for a sustained gap between the work and the person that prayer and coaching and time have not closed, when you have named it clearly more than once and given a real path and watched the path go unwalked. Fire for character, faster than you want to, because a gifted manipulator does more damage in a church than an honest underperformer ever will. Fire when keeping someone requires you to lie, to the elders about how it is going, to the congregation about why numbers are slipping, to the person himself about a future that is not coming. The lie is the signal. When you are lying to keep the peace, the peace is already gone.

The history of how we got so timid is worth tracing. The professionalization of ministry, which gathered speed across the twentieth century and accelerated after the church growth movement of the nineteen seventies built the multi-staff church, gave us employees without giving us the stomach to manage them. We borrowed the human resources department's vocabulary, the performance plan and the documented warning, but we kept a theology of the pastorate that treats every staff member as an ordained brother whose removal is a kind of excommunication. So we freeze. We have the corporate tools and the covenantal nerves, and the two cancel out, and the failing leader stays for three years while everyone suffers and calls it love.

Edwin Friedman saw this paralysis everywhere he looked, and he named its real cause. He said the chronically anxious system will always pressure the leader to relieve its anxiety, and the most anxious members will set the agenda, so the leader who cannot tolerate someone else's pain will be ruled by whoever is most willing to inflict it on him (Friedman 2007). The pastor who cannot fire is not more loving. He is less differentiated. He has let the discomfort of one hard conversation hold an entire church hostage. The failure of nerve does not look like failure. It looks like patience. That is what makes it so durable.

Here is the reversal that took me too long to learn. The kindest thing is almost always the earlier thing. The longer you wait, the worse the eventual conversation gets for everyone, especially the person you are protecting. Keep a man two years past the point of fit and you have not given him grace, you have given him two years of failing publicly, two years of his confidence eroding, two years of a marriage straining under a job he cannot do, before you finally say what you could have said with dignity at month nine. Delay does not soften the blow. It compounds it and then delivers it anyway, with interest he had no idea he was accruing.

When the day comes, do it the way Jesus moved on the last night, from security and not from anger. He knew where his authority came from and so he could kneel and serve even Judas (John 13:3-5 ESV). You can deliver hard news with that kind of steadiness only if you are not secretly trying to make the other person agree that you are fair. Tell the truth plainly. Own your part in waiting too long. Be generous with severance and time and a real reference, because how you end a tenure preaches to everyone still on staff about what you actually believe. Ruth Haley Barton writes that leaders have to attend to their own souls precisely so that their decisions flow from God and not from their own unexamined fear (Barton 2008). The firing done from a settled soul is a different act than the firing done from panic, even when the words are the same.

There is one more place we hide, and it is the holiest-sounding excuse of all. We say we are waiting on the Lord. We say we have not yet received clarity, that we are praying for wisdom, that we do not want to run ahead of God. And sometimes that is true and good. But often the language of discernment is the language of paralysis with a stained-glass window in front of it. Ruth Haley Barton writes that we have to be honest about the difference between genuine waiting on God and the spiritualized procrastination that lets us avoid a decision we already know we have to make (Barton 2008). The Spirit who gave us wisdom also gave us the courage to act on it. When the clarity has been sitting in your chest for six months and you are still calling it discernment, the thing you are waiting on is not God. It is your own willingness to be disliked.

The goal was never to be a man who can fire easily. The goal is to be a man who can tell the truth in love when love and truth both cost something. Most of us are not too quick to let people go. We are too slow, and we baptize the slowness, and the people we claim to be protecting pay for our comfort.

Grace tells the truth in time. Cowardice waits for it to die.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

title: Leading Through Conflict on a Church Team
excerpt: A church team does not get into trouble because it fights, it gets into trouble because it learned to call avoidance peace.
body:
Two staff members have not directly spoken to each other in four months, and everyone knows it, and nobody says it. They are professionals. They pass each other in the hall. They sit on the same row in the all-staff meeting and route every actual message through a third person who has become an unwilling diplomat between two people who used to be friends. The team is functioning. The calendar fills, the services happen, the bulletin gets printed. And underneath the function a low current of avoidance is running through everything, and the longer it runs the more the whole team organizes itself around not setting it off.

We have a strange relationship with conflict in the church. We treat it as a failure of sanctification, as if a mature team would simply never disagree, as if the presence of friction proves the absence of the Spirit. So when conflict shows up, and it always shows up, we feel ashamed of it and we hide it. We swallow the disagreement and call the swallowing humility. We let the resentment build and call the building patience. And the conflict does not go anywhere. It just moves down, out of the meeting and into the body, into the headaches and the clipped emails and the Sunday smiles that do not reach the eyes.

Let me steel-man the peacemaker, because he is quoting Jesus and he is not wrong about much. Blessed are the peacemakers. A quarrelsome church is a poor witness, and the world is watching how we treat each other, and Paul begged the Philippians to be of the same mind. The peacemaker has seen what unchecked conflict does, has watched a church split over a building program and never recover, has buried friendships that died in a business meeting. His instinct to protect the unity of the team is not cowardice. It is the scar tissue of someone who has seen the alternative. He is guarding something he has watched bleed out before.

But he has misread the text he is standing on, and the misreading is costing him the very thing he wants. Peacemaking is not peacekeeping. The peacemaker in the Sermon on the Mount is an active figure who goes into the broken place and makes something, the way a steelworker makes a beam, through heat and pressure and joining. The peacekeeper is a different creature entirely. He keeps the peace by keeping the lid on, and the lid is not peace, it is a delay. What he calls unity is two people not speaking for four months while a third carries their mail. Jesus did not bless that. He blessed the harder and braver thing, the one that walks into the conflict on purpose and stays until something is actually mended.

The spine text is plainer than we admit, and it is from Jesus' own mouth. 'If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone' (Matthew 18:15 ESV). Go. The movement is toward the person, not away. Alone, which means not to the third party, not to the prayer chain disguised as concern, not to the spouse over dinner, not to the loose coalition you are quietly building in the hallway. The most disobeyed verse in church staff life is not about money or sex or doctrine. It is this one, the simple command to take the problem to the person and nobody else, and our entire architecture of avoidance exists to get around it.

Watch what triangulation actually does to a team, because it is the disease underneath most church conflict. Edwin Friedman built his whole understanding of congregations on the way anxiety moves through relationships, and he showed that when two people cannot tolerate the tension between them, they will reliably pull in a third to stabilize it (Friedman 2007). The third person feels useful, even chosen, carrying messages and absorbing complaints. But the triangle does not resolve the conflict. It preserves it. It lets two people stay angry indefinitely because the pressure that would have forced them to deal with each other is being bled off through someone else. Every staff has these triangles. Most pastors are sitting inside several of them and feeling needed instead of feeling alarmed.

We did not invent this avoidance. We inherited it, and the history clarifies the grip it has. The therapeutic turn in American culture, which the sociologist Philip Rieff diagnosed as early as nineteen sixty-six in his account of the triumph of the therapeutic, taught us to read every relational difficulty as a matter of feelings to be managed and validated rather than truths to be told (Rieff 1966). The church drank deeply from that stream. We learned to prize emotional comfort above honest correction, to fear hurting someone more than we feared leaving them in sin, to mistake niceness for love. A whole generation of church teams now treats the avoidance of hard words as the highest relational virtue, and we cannot find the verse that taught us that, because there is no such verse.

Here is the reversal. The conflict you are avoiding is not the threat to the team. The avoidance is the threat. Lencioni mapped this with uncomfortable precision when he showed that teams which cannot engage in honest conflict do not become more unified, they become less committed, because people will not buy into a decision they were never allowed to argue with (Lencioni 2002). The silence you are protecting is producing the disengagement you are about to complain about. The meeting where nobody pushes back is not a sign of alignment. It is the sound of people who have stopped believing their voice changes anything, saving their real opinions for the parking lot where the decisions get quietly unmade.

So lead into it. When you sense the four-month silence, name it out loud and decline to be the third corner of the triangle, sending the two people back to each other with your blessing and your expectation. When someone comes to complain about a colleague, the most pastoral question you can ask is whether they have said this to the person directly, and the most pastoral answer to no is to walk with them until they do. Set the table so that conflict in the meeting is normal and conflict in the hallway is not. The team that fights well in the open is the team that does not need to fight in the dark.

And remember whose night this pattern comes from. On the last evening, with betrayal already in the room and the disciples still arguing about which of them was greatest, Jesus did not lecture them about unity. He knelt and washed their feet, including the feet of the man who would sell him (John 13:4-5 ESV). The model for leading through conflict is not a technique. It is a posture, the willingness to get low and serve people you are in genuine tension with, to stay in the room and stay tender at the same time. Nouwen called this the downward movement of Christian leadership, the refusal to escape conflict through power, the choice to remain present and vulnerable where it would be easier to dominate or disappear (Nouwen 1989).

I have to name my own part in this, because I led a team for years that I was proud of for never fighting, and I have since come to understand that I was proud of the wrong thing. The reason nobody fought in my meetings was not that we had achieved some rare maturity. It was that I had made disagreement expensive, in a hundred small ways I never noticed, and my people had done the arithmetic and decided silence was cheaper. The peace I prized was the peace of a room that had given up on changing my mind. It took a staff member leaving, and telling me on the way out the things she had never felt safe to say while she stayed, before I understood that the quiet I had treated as a trophy was actually the bill coming due. I had mistaken the absence of conflict for the presence of unity, and the two had never been further apart.

A team that has learned to fight honestly and stay is more unified than a team that has never fought at all, the way a bone that healed is stronger than a bone that was never tested. We keep protecting our teams from the one thing that would actually bind them together. We keep choosing the quiet, and the quiet keeps costing us the thing the quiet was supposed to save.

Peace is not the absence of conflict. It is conflict carried all the way through.

### Works Cited

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Lencioni, Patrick. 2002. The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

Rieff, Philip. 1966. The Triumph of the Therapeutic: Uses of Faith After Freud. New York: Harper and Row.

title: How to Develop Leaders, Not Just Recruit Volunteers
excerpt: A church can run a hundred volunteers through its slots for a decade and produce not a single leader, and most of them do.
body:
Every September the same announcement goes up on the screen and into the bulletin and across the platform. We need volunteers. The nursery is short, the parking team is thin, the connections desk has two people doing the work of five, and so the ask goes out, and a few tired saints raise their hands again because they always do. The church fills its slots. The machine runs another year. And if you stood at the back of that room and asked who among these faithful people is being formed into a leader who could one day carry weight, the honest answer would be almost none of them, because nobody is trying to.

There is a difference between recruiting and developing, and most churches have collapsed it without noticing. Recruiting fills a need that the church has. Developing meets a need that the person has, the need to grow into the fullness of what God made them to carry. Recruiting asks what the volunteer can do for the ministry. Developing asks what the ministry can do for the volunteer, what God might be building in a human being through the assignment. We say we want to develop leaders. What we usually want is to fill the schedule, and the schedule, once filled, has no reason to develop anyone.

Let me make the recruiter's case honestly, because the work is real and the recruiter is not lazy. The services do have to happen. The children do have to be safe. Someone does have to count the offering and run the slides and stack the chairs, and a church that romanticizes development while the practical work falls apart is not deep, it is just disorganized. The recruiter is keeping the lights on. He looks at the gap between the work and the workers and he closes it the only way he knows how, week after week, and the church owes him more thanks than it gives. His instinct to staff the need is not wrong.

But he has accepted a quiet exchange that is hollowing his church out from the inside. By treating people as labor to be deployed, he gets the slot filled this week and loses the leader who would have filled a hundred slots over twenty years. He is harvesting and never planting. And there is a deeper cost, because people can tell when they are being used rather than formed. The volunteer who senses that the church only wants his hands and not his growth eventually burns out, not from the labor but from the meaninglessness of labor that leads nowhere. We wonder why we cannot keep volunteers. It is because we never made them into anything. We just spent them.

The text I want to carry is the way Jesus made leaders, because it is almost the opposite of how we do it. 'And he appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach' (Mark 3:14 ESV). Read the order. With him first. Sent out second. The being with came before the doing for, and the doing flowed out of the being with. Jesus did not recruit twelve volunteers to staff a movement. He drew twelve men into his life, let them watch him pray and weep and argue and rest, and only out of that shared life did he send them to do anything. The formation was relational before it was functional. We have inverted the order, and the inversion is the whole problem.

The history of how we lost this is the history of the church learning to think like a business, and the year markers are not subtle. When the church growth movement took hold across the nineteen seventies and eighties, and Peter Drucker, the most influential management thinker of the century, began consulting with megachurch pastors and teaching them to run congregations as organizations to be scaled, we gained efficiency and lost apprenticeship. The org chart replaced the rabbi. We built systems to process volunteers at scale, intake forms and ministry placement matrices and the language of human capital, and a system that processes people efficiently is structurally incapable of doing the slow, inefficient, deeply personal work of forming one leader at a time. The factory cannot raise a child.

Here is the reversal that costs the most to accept. Developing leaders will always look less efficient than recruiting volunteers, and it will always produce more in the end. Pouring eighteen months into one person who might lead a ministry someday is a worse use of a Tuesday than filling six open slots, by every metric your dashboard tracks. But the six slots are filled by people who will leave, and the one person becomes someone who fills slots you will never see, who develops others, who is still leading when you are gone. The kingdom does not scale the way a corporation scales. It scales the way a vineyard scales, slowly, through roots, one planting at a time, and you will not see the harvest in the quarter you planted it.

What does developing actually require of us, and why do we avoid it. It requires proximity, the willingness to let people close enough to watch you lead and to be coached inside the real work rather than in a classroom. Ruth Haley Barton argues that leaders can only give away what they themselves have received, that an unformed leader produces unformed followers, that the inner life of the one doing the developing is the ceiling on everyone he develops (Barton 2008). This is why we avoid it. Developing a leader means being watched up close, and being watched up close means being known, and being known means our own gaps come into view. Recruiting keeps people at arm's length. Developing brings them inside, where they can see us, and that is precisely the cost we do not want to pay.

It also requires that we hand over real authority before the person is fully ready, which terrifies the recruiter, because real authority handed over means real mistakes made in public. But there is no other way it has ever worked. Jesus sent the twelve out while they still misunderstood almost everything, and they came back having done the work badly and well, and the sending was the school. We hoard the meaningful decisions and then wonder why nobody around us has grown. You cannot develop a leader by letting him stack chairs. You develop him by letting him lead, and then standing close enough to debrief the wreckage and the wins, week after week, until the day he is leading better than you.

The deepest part is the part we are most tempted to skip, the formation of the person beneath the function. Bonhoeffer reminded us that Christian community is not an ideal we impose but a reality we receive, that the goal is never to build the impressive thing but to serve the actual person God has placed in front of us (Bonhoeffer 1954). Developing a leader is finally an act of love for that specific human being, not a strategy for staffing the church. The moment it becomes a strategy, the person feels it, and the formation dies. We must want the volunteer to grow even if it means he grows right out of our church and into a calling we never get the credit for.

The last picture is the towel again, because it is always the towel. Jesus formed leaders by getting on the floor and washing their feet, by showing them that the greatness they kept arguing about was found at the bottom and not the top (John 13:14-15 ESV). You will not develop leaders from behind a desk handing out assignments. You develop them by descending into the work beside them and letting them watch you choose the lowest seat on purpose. That is the curriculum. There is no other one.

There is a final cost most of us never count, and it is the cost to our own ego. The leader who develops other leaders is signing up to be eclipsed. The people you raise well will, if you have done it faithfully, eventually preach better than you preached at their age, lead larger than you led, see things you cannot see. And a great deal of what passes for a shortage of leaders in our churches is actually a senior leader's quiet unwillingness to be surpassed, a hoarding of the spotlight dressed up as a concern for readiness. We keep people in the volunteer pool because a developed leader is a threat to the man at the top in a way a chair-stacker never will be. Nouwen warned that the descending way of Jesus runs directly against the climbing instinct that lives in every leader, that we are forever tempted to grasp at relevance and visibility instead of giving them away (Nouwen 1989). You cannot develop a leader and protect your own prominence at the same time. You have to choose, and most of us choose ourselves and call it prudence.

A church that only recruits will always be short of volunteers. A church that develops will one day have more leaders than it knows what to do with. Almost all of us are running the first kind and praying for the results of the second.

Stop filling slots. Start raising leaders.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

title: The Lonely Seat: Power and the Senior Leader
excerpt: The loneliness of the senior seat is real, and the way most pastors try to cure it is exactly what makes it worse.
body:
A pastor stands at the door after the third service, and forty people tell him it was exactly what they needed, and he drives home and cannot think of a single person he could call to say he is not okay. He leads a staff of twelve. He has elders who pray for him by name. He is surrounded all week by people who depend on him, who admire him, who would say without hesitation that they love him. And he is alone in a way that none of them can see, because the seat he sits in has put a pane of glass between him and everyone who reports to him, and he installed the glass himself and forgot he did it.

The loneliness of the senior leader is one of the most documented and least discussed facts of ministry. Pastors leave the work in great numbers, and when they are asked why, isolation appears near the top of the list, ahead of money and ahead of conflict. We acknowledge this loneliness with a kind of sympathy that does nothing, the way we acknowledge that the work is hard. What we rarely do is look at where the loneliness comes from, because the source is uncomfortable. The loneliness of the senior seat is not only something done to the leader. It is largely something the leader does to himself, through power, and the cure he reaches for makes it worse.

Let me steel-man the leader who keeps his distance, because his reasons are not foolish and I have used every one of them. He will tell you, correctly, that he cannot be fully transparent with people he supervises, that there are confidences he must keep, that a leader who falls apart in front of his team destabilizes the whole team. He will tell you that authority requires a measure of separateness, that the captain cannot drink with the crew, that someone has to carry what cannot be shared. And he is right about all of it. The seat does require a real and necessary solitude. Some of the distance is the cost of the office, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty.

But he has done something with that legitimate truth that turns it into a prison. He has taken the necessary solitude of the role and quietly expanded it into a total isolation that serves his power rather than his people. There is a difference between the loneliness that comes from carrying confidences and the loneliness that comes from never letting anyone see you need anything. The first is the cost of leadership. The second is the fruit of pride dressed as duty. He has confused them on purpose, because the second kind protects an image, and the image has become more precious to him than the relationships, and he calls the whole thing the loneliness of command when half of it is the loneliness of self-protection.

The text I want to carry is the one we read every Maundy Thursday and rarely apply to ourselves. On the last night, knowing that all things had been given into his hands, Jesus took off his outer garments and knelt to wash the feet of his friends (John 13:3-5 ESV). The one with the most power in the room made himself the most exposed. He did not use his authority to elevate himself above the table. He used it to descend below it, to take the servant's place, to let twelve men see their teacher on the floor. Power, in the hands of the one who held the most of it, became the freedom to be vulnerable. That is the exact opposite of what power usually does to us, and it is the medicine for the lonely seat.

Because here is what power does to most of us, and the social science is as old as the church's amnesia about it. Edwin Friedman observed that leaders become isolated not primarily because others push them away but because they stop being honestly engaged, hiding behind the role, managing impressions, surrounding themselves with people who will not contradict them (Friedman 2007). The lonely leader has often, without admitting it, selected for agreement. He has promoted the people who affirm him and grown cool toward the ones who push, and over years he has built a court rather than a team, and a court is the loneliest place on earth because everyone in it is performing for the king. The isolation he laments is the harvest of choices he made one staffing decision at a time.

The history here runs deep and it indicts our whole model. The cult of the singular visionary pastor, the leader as charismatic founder whose voice cannot be questioned, took its modern shape in the church growth movement of the nineteen seventies and eighties and hardened into the celebrity pastor era that followed. We built churches around one magnetic personality and then watched, decade after decade, as those personalities fell, in moral collapse and in burnout and in the slow corrosion of men who had no peers because they had been elevated above everyone they knew. The architecture that made them powerful is the same architecture that made them alone. We keep building it. We keep being surprised when it produces the same wreckage it has always produced.

Henri Nouwen saw the spiritual mechanism under all of it, and he named the temptation with a precision that still stings. He wrote that the great seduction of Christian leadership is the temptation to power, to be the one in control, and that this temptation is so dangerous precisely because it is so easy to confuse the desire to rule with the desire to serve (Nouwen 1989). The antidote he prescribed was not better self-protection or more self-care. It was confession and community, the deliberate placing of oneself among people to whom one is accountable and before whom one is known, the refusal to lead alone. The lonely pastor has often medicated his loneliness with more control, and control is the drug that deepens the disease it pretends to treat.

Here is the reversal, and it is the hinge of everything. The solution to the loneliness of power is not more power and it is not less responsibility. It is vulnerability exercised from within the power, the John 13 move, the choice to let someone see you while you still hold the authority. This is terrifying, because we believe that to be seen as needy is to forfeit the right to lead. The cross says the reverse. The one who knelt with the towel did not lose his authority by descending. He revealed it. Authority that cannot kneel is not authority, it is insecurity holding a title, and everyone on the staff can feel the difference even when they cannot name it.

What this asks of us is concrete and costly. It asks the senior leader to build, on purpose, a set of relationships outside his chain of command where he is not the pastor but simply a man who needs God, peers who can tell him the truth because their livelihood does not depend on his mood. It asks him to find a spiritual director or a soul friend, what Ruth Haley Barton calls the company of others who will help him discern his own deceptions, because the leader cannot see his own blind spots by definition and will go down with them if no one is permitted close enough to point (Barton 2008). And it asks him to stop curating a staff of admirers and start keeping the people who push back, treating their resistance as a gift instead of a threat.

I have lived on both sides of the glass, and the difference is not subtle once you have felt it. There were years when I told myself the distance between me and my staff was the dignity of the office, and what it actually was, underneath, was fear of being found out, the dread that if anyone got close enough they would discover I was less than the man who stood on the platform. So I kept everyone at the range of admiration, which is a safe and lonely range, and I mistook the safety for wisdom. What broke it was not a strategy. It was a few men outside my church who refused to be impressed by me, who asked how my marriage was and would not accept the sermon-version of the answer, and who slowly taught me that being known by a few is the only thing that makes being admired by many survivable. Bonhoeffer wrote that the person who cannot bear to be alone should beware of community, and that the person who cannot bear community should beware of being alone, because we need both and we will be destroyed by whichever one we use to flee the other (Bonhoeffer 1954). The lonely leader has used the crowd to flee the few, and it is killing him by the inch.

The lonely seat will not be cured by sympathy and it will not be cured by stepping down. It will be cured, if it is cured at all, by the slow and humbling work of letting yourself be known by people you cannot control, which is the only kind of being known that counts. Most of us would rather stay lonely than do that, because the loneliness, for all its pain, lets us keep the image intact. We choose the glass. We sit behind it and ache and call it the price of leadership, when half the time it is the price of pride.

The man who knelt with the towel was never alone in the way we are. Put down the power you are hiding behind, and you might not be either.
